title: Greetings and names
goal: Greet people, say your name and say where you're from — in two speech levels at once, so you see from the very first minute that ngoko and krama are not two languages but two vocabularies on top of one grammar.
bekal: greet friends your own age in ngoko and older people in krama
say your name and where you're from with *jenengku* / *nami kula* and *saka* / *saking*
use six personal pronouns with one and the same verb form

dialogs.title: Dialogue 1 — Ing koridor kos (ngoko)
dialogs.intro: It's Dian's first day at a boarding house (*kos*) in Sagan, a neighborhood of Yogyakarta. She is opening her door when a young woman her age comes out of the next room carrying a bucket.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Éh, kowé sing kamar telu, ya?
lines.id: Hey, you're the one in room three, right?
lines.literal: eh, you who room three, yes?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Aku Rini. Kamarku sebelah. Kowé wong ngendi?
lines.id: I'm Rini. My room's next door. Where are you from?
lines.literal: I Rini. room-my next-door. you person where?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Aku saka Jakarta. Aku mahasiswa anyar ing kéné.
lines.id: I'm from Jakarta. I'm a new student here.
lines.literal: I from Jakarta. I student new at here.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Wah, adoh, ya. Aku wong Klaten.
lines.id: Wow, that's far. I'm from Klaten.
lines.literal: wow, far, yes. I person Klaten.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Apik-apik waé. Kowé bisa basa Jawa?
lines.literal: good-good just. you can language Javanese?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Ya wis, ngobrol nganggo basa Jawa waé, ya?
lines.id: Well then, let's just chat in Javanese, OK?
lines.literal: yes already, chat using language Javanese just, yes?

notes: **Aku Dian** — "I Dian", with no word for *am*. Javanese has no linking verb in sentences like this. *Aku mahasiswa* (I [am a] student), *aku wong Klaten*, *kamarku sebelah*: you simply put the parts side by side.

**Jenengku** and **kamarku** — the owner is attached to the **end** of the word instead of standing in front of it. The endings are *-ku* (my), *-mu* (your), and *-é* or *-né* (his/her, or "the"): *jenengku* = my name, *kamarmu* = your room.

**Kowé** is pronounced **ko-WAY**. Use it with friends your age and with younger people. With older people or people you've just met, switch to *sampeyan* (fairly polite) or *panjenengan* (fully polite) — and once you use either, the other words in the sentence usually move up to krama too.

**Wong ngendi** is literally "person where". To ask where someone is from, Javanese uses this pattern more often than "from where". The answer matches it: *aku wong Klaten*, "I'm a Klaten person". If you'd rather use "from": *aku saka Jakarta*.
**Piyé** (how) has several twins that mean exactly the same: *kepriyé*, *keprié*, and in some areas *kepiyé*. All are correct; *piyé* is the one you'll hear most. Its krama form is *kadospundi*.
**Apik-apik waé** — the doubled word means "so-so, nothing special", softened by *waé* ("just"). It's the standard answer to *piyé kabaré?*, as automatic as "fine, thanks" in English.

**Matur nuwun** is the "thank you" that's safe at every level — with friends and with people you respect. The short form is just *nuwun*, and the most casual is *suwun*. For extra respect: *matur nuwun sanget* (thank you very much).

grammars.title: Verbs don't change for the person
body: This is why Javanese grammar feels light. Read the table from top to bottom and notice that the last three columns don't move at all.
after: No *am/is/are*, no *-s* for he/she, no six-line conjugation table. One form for everyone: "I eat, he eat, they eat".

Notice that **"we" and "they" aren't single words** but phrases. *Awaké dhéwé* is literally "our own body", and *dhèwèké kabèh* is "he/she all". Javanese also uses *kita* (we, borrowed from Indonesian, used freely) and *padha* to mark a plural doer: *padha mangan* — "(they) all eat".
**Dhèwèké** doesn't distinguish male from female — it means both "he" and "she". The short form *dèké* is also common.

dialogs.title: Dialogue 2 — Ing ngarep kos (krama)
dialogs.intro: That afternoon Dian meets a man in his sixties sweeping the yard. He turns out to be the owner of the boarding house. Notice that the conversation is almost exactly the same as the first one — only the vocabulary changes.

lines.speaker: Pak Broto:
lines.text: Sugeng sonten, Mbak. Panjenengan ingkang énggal?
lines.id: Good afternoon, Miss. Are you the new one?
lines.literal: good afternoon, Miss. you who new?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Yes, sir. My name is Dian.

lines.speaker: Pak Broto:
lines.text: Kula Broto, ingkang gadhah kos menika.
lines.id: I'm Broto, the owner of this boarding house.
lines.literal: I Broto, who own boarding-house this.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Kula saking Jakarta. Kula mahasiswi énggal.
lines.id: I'm from Jakarta. I'm a new student.
lines.literal: I from Jakarta. I student new.

lines.speaker: Pak Broto:
lines.text: O, tebih. Sugeng rawuh ing Ngayogyakarta.
lines.id: Oh, that's far. Welcome to Yogyakarta.
lines.literal: oh, far. blessed arrival in Yogyakarta.

notes: Compare the two dialogues word for word and you'll see that **the sentence patterns are identical**. *Kowé wong ngendi?* and *Panjenengan saking pundi?* are built the same way: pronoun first, question word at the end. Only the word choice changes.

**Sugeng** opens every krama greeting and good wish: *sugeng énjing* (morning), *sugeng siyang* (midday), *sugeng sonten* (afternoon), *sugeng dalu* (night), *sugeng rawuh* (welcome), *sugeng tindak* (have a good trip, to someone leaving), *sugeng pinanggih* (nice to meet you), *sugeng sinau* (happy studying). One word, ten greetings. Mbak and Pak are polite address words for a young woman and an older man.
**Inggih** is the krama "yes", the partner of *iya*. It's used constantly, often repeated (*inggih, inggih*), and often on its own to show you're listening — like "mm-hm, yes" in English.

**Panjenengan** is the most respectful "you". One step below it is *sampeyan*, for someone a little older or your equal whom you don't know well. With Pak Broto, who is much older, *panjenengan* is right.

**Kula** replaces *aku* in krama. There are even humbler forms, *kawula* and *dalem*, but they sound very formal — used in speeches, at the royal court, or to someone of far higher standing. For everyday life, *kula* is enough.
**Ngayogyakarta** is the official Javanese name of Yogyakarta. In daily life people say *Jogja* or *Yogya* — no need for the long form.

grammars.title: Same sentence, two levels
body: Keep this table. It holds the whole of Unit 1 in one place, and you'll see the same pattern repeat in the next nineteen units.
after: The second-to-last row hides a small surprise: **even "Javanese" has a krama form, *Jawi***. So do the names of some places and frequently mentioned things. Don't chase them now — just know they exist.

You may have noticed that **ora** and **boten** haven't appeared in any dialogue yet. They're placed here on purpose because you'll need them tomorrow: these two words negate anything in Javanese, and there's no other form to memorize.

blocks.text: Time-of-day greetings in Javanese **exist only in krama**. There's no ngoko version, and that's not a gap — Javanese people simply don't say "good morning" to friends their age. They say *piyé?* (how's it going?) or *arep menyang ngendi?* (where are you off to?), or just call the person's name.
The reply is the same greeting, handed straight back: if someone says *sugeng énjing*, you answer *sugeng énjing*. That's all there is to it.

**Nuwun sèwu** literally means "I ask a thousand" — a thousand pardons. Use it to squeeze past someone, to interrupt, and to open a question to a stranger. If you can memorize only three Javanese words today, make this one of them: it opens almost every conversation in Java.

sections.title: Why this first unit feels easy

blocks.text: The first unit of most language courses already crashes you into a grammar wall. Here there's no wall, and that's no accident — Javanese simply doesn't have four things that make other languages hard:

items: **Verbs don't change for the person.** *Aku mangan, kowé mangan, dhèwèké mangan* — I eat, you eat, she eat. One form, always.
**No special "-ing" form.** If you need to show something is in progress, just add *lagi*: *aku sinau* (I study) → *aku lagi sinau* (I'm studying). The verb itself never changes.
**No articles.** No *the*, no *a*. *Omah* can mean "house", "a house" or "the house" as needed; if you need to be specific, the ending *-é* does it: *omahé*, "the house".

**Familiar word order.** Doer, verb, object, as in English; but adjectives come after the noun (*omah gedhé*, house big = a big house), and question words stay where the answer would go (*kowé wong ngendi?*, you person where?).

blocks.text: Only **one** thing is truly new — undha-usuk, the speech levels — and this course starts it in Unit 1 precisely because it's the one thing that takes time. The rest is vocabulary, and vocabulary comes by itself through repetition.

blocks.title: Don't be afraid to mix
items: If you run out of krama words mid-sentence, don't stop — slip in an ngoko (or even Indonesian) word and keep going. Javanese speakers do it every day.

What you must **not** mix is switching from *panjenengan* or *sampeyan* to *kowé* in the middle of a conversation with an older person. Pronouns are what people hear most. Guard that one, and the rest is forgiven.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right pronoun. (Hint: the verb never needs to change.)
Change these ngoko sentences into krama.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: Aku — Kowé — Dhèwèké — kula — Panjenengan — Dhèwèké
Kula saking Jakarta. — Nami panjenengan sinten? — Panjenengan saking pundi? — Inggih, leres. — Kula boten saged basa Jawi. — Griya kula tebih.
Jenengku Ahmad. — Aku wong Klaten. — Kowé mahasiswa anyar? — Piyé kabaré? — Aku lagi sinau sithik. — Sesuk manèh!
Jenengku Dian. — Kowé wong ngendi? — Aku saka Jakarta. — Aku lagi sinau basa Jawa. — Panjenengan saking pundi?
